why: In a script, reads go in text order (the user's ruling 3), and a clear ends the writes of exactly the names it removes (MATLAB doc 'clear', 'clearvars'; R2026a: `clear global zg` removes `zg` only, `clear xa*` the names matching): `clearvars -except y` removes `x` and keeps `y`; `clear xa*` removes `xa`, not `x`; `clear -regexp ^xb` removes `xb`, not `w`; `clear -regexp mq` removes `xmq` (a regular expression matches anywhere in the name), not `w`; `clear x*z` removes `x1z`, not `x1za` (a wildcard matches the whole name); `clearvars xj* -except xjk` removes `xj1`, not `xjk`; `clear global zg` removes `zg`, not `y`; `clear functions` removes no variable; `clear classes` removes every one. `clear global` alone removes the global variables, the names declared `global` before it, and no other (doc 'clear': "clear global removes all global variables"): it keeps `q` and removes `gq`, and a name declared global after it stays. So each removed name read after is a call of its function, and each kept one indexes the variable. A clear whose names are built at run time (`clear(n)`) may remove any name: no write reaches through it (project rule).
